summary.one_line: A dominant Indian supplier of SBR wastewater-treatment technology (claimed >80% share) with steady ~29% EBITDA margins, but almost no profit has turned into cash over three years, 92%+ of its business depends on government-funded projects, and 77.5% of this Rs.667.5 crore IPO is an offer for sale. The fresh Rs.150 crore mostly pays down debt and funds working capital.
bull_points: Real niche leadership: the RHP's industry report credits SFC with over 80% market share in sequencing batch reactor (SBR) technology in India, with 728 wastewater installations treating about 17,511 MLD as of July 2026 (S15, S10, S2).
Margins have held steady: operating EBITDA margin was 29.39%, 29.73% and 29.34% in FY24-FY26, and revenue grew at a 10.56% CAGR to Rs.803.6 crore (S2).
Asset-light model: fixed-asset turnover is 12-13x, because SFC supplies the technology and core equipment while EPC contractors do the civil construction (S2).
Order book roughly tripled from Rs.560.4 crore (FY25) to Rs.1,574.5 crore (FY26) and stood at Rs.1,570.1 crore in June 2026. That is about 2x FY26 revenue (S2).
Repeat customers made up 91.98% of FY26 revenue, which suggests EPC contractors keep coming back to the C-Tech platform (S10).
bear_points: Profits are not turning into cash: operating cash flow over FY24-FY26 totalled about Rs.28 crore against cumulative PAT of about Rs.456 crore, and it was negative again (-Rs.21.3 crore) in Q1 FY27 (S2).
Working capital keeps growing: the cash conversion cycle went from 156 to 242 days between FY24 and FY26, and working capital rose from 39.9% to 65.2% of revenue (S2).
Borrowings more than doubled, from Rs.83.7 crore (FY25) to Rs.195.6 crore (FY26) and Rs.204.8 crore by June 2026. Net debt turned positive (S2).

The issue is 77.5% OFS (Rs.517.5 crore). Promoter Dhandoriya, executive director Sarvesh Garg and early shareholders are selling large stakes at a weighted average acquisition cost of Rs.36.72 per share (S2, S7).
Government dependence: government-linked work was 92.35% of FY26 WWT revenue and 100% of SWT revenue, and top-5 customer share rose from 40.5% (FY24) to 62.1% (Q1 FY27) (S2).

Governance flags in the RHP itself: some corporate records are 'not traceable or have certain discrepancies', and a German subsidiary faces EUR 6.25 million (about Rs.66.7 crore) of material civil litigation (S2).
watch_points: Whether FY27 operating cash flow finally turns meaningfully positive, which is the single most important test of earnings quality (S2).
Conversion of the Rs.1,570 crore order book, especially the newer WRR (Rs.561 crore) and SWT/compressed-biogas orders, into revenue and cash (S11, S10).
Outcome of the EUR 6.25 million civil litigation at SFC Umwelttechnik GmbH and the 10 regulatory proceedings against subsidiaries (S2).
Anchor lock-in expiries: 50% of anchor shares on 29 Nov 2026 and the rest on 28 Jan 2027 (S7).
Final-day QIB demand: QIB bids were only 0.08x as of the evening of day 2 (S8).

reasoning: The moat is real but narrow. A claimed >80% share of India's SBR wastewater technology market, built on 728 installations, is a genuine installed-base and specification advantage with EPC contractors (S15, S2). It sits inside government sewage-treatment budgets, though, and 92%+ of WWT revenue ultimately depends on government awards (S2).

Earnings quality is the deciding problem. Rs.456 crore of cumulative PAT over FY24-FY26 produced only about Rs.28 crore of operating cash, and the cash conversion cycle widened from 156 to 242 days (S2). Until reported profits show up as cash, the 20-22% PAT margins cannot be taken at face value.

The fresh money fixes the balance sheet rather than funding growth. Of Rs.150 crore fresh issue, Rs.42.2 crore repays borrowings and Rs.74.9 crore funds working capital, which plugs the cash gap created by slow collections. No capacity or technology capex is funded (S2, S7).

Insiders are cashing out. 77.5% of the issue is OFS, and a promoter-director and an executive director are selling roughly 44% and 64% of their holdings at a weighted acquisition cost of Rs.36.72 (S2, S7). Promoter-group holding falls from 48.18% to 41.18% (S7).

Governance and litigation are not clean enough to overlook: untraceable or discrepant corporate records, a criminal-proceeding notice naming the CMD, and Rs.69.3 crore of claims against subsidiaries, mostly German litigation (S2). These are manageable, not disqualifying, but they add to the cash-flow concern.

This is worth tracking rather than avoiding outright, because the business itself (niche technology leadership, steady margins, a 2x revenue order book) is sound (S2). A year of listed disclosures showing positive operating cash flow and stable receivables would materially change the case.

blocks.text: SFC Environmental Technologies, incorporated in 2005 and headquartered in Vashi, Navi Mumbai, describes itself as an environmental technology company. It works in three areas: wastewater treatment (WWT), wastewater recycling and reuse (WRR), and solid waste treatment (SWT) (S2, S10). In wastewater, SFC usually does not build the plant. It designs the process, manufactures and supplies the core treatment equipment, and supervises installation and commissioning. The EPC contractor that won the municipal tender does the civil construction (S15, S16).

The core product is C-Tech, a proprietary sequencing batch reactor (SBR) platform for sewage and industrial effluent. As of July 31, 2026, SFC technology had been delivered to 728 WWT installations across 23 states and five Union Territories, treating about 17,511 million litres per day (S2, S15, S10). The RHP's KPI table shows the installed base growing from 577 installations and 13,907 MLD (FY24) to 705 and 17,144 MLD (FY26) (S2).

In WRR, SFC sells tertiary treatment such as ultrafiltration, closed-circuit reverse osmosis and membrane bioreactors. It signed an exclusive supply agreement with DuPont in August 2024 (S10, S18). The segment is new: it booked Rs.14.2 crore of revenue in FY26 and nothing in other periods (S2). In SWT, SFC uses its OREX technology to separate organic waste for biogas recovery, and through subsidiaries it runs two integrated municipal solid waste plants in North and South Goa under a public-private partnership (S2, S10, S16).

items: Vertical integration: decanter manufacturing in Pune (2022), diffusers through subsidiary Fine Aeration Systems, and a turbo-blower joint venture, Turbomax India (2023) (S12).
Process automation: subsidiary Chavare Engineering designs and makes control panels, PLCs and power panels. It is reported as 'other operating revenue' (S2).
Europe: majority stake in SFC Umwelttechnik GmbH since 2008, and 80% of Germany's IST-Anlagenbau (solar sludge drying), acquired in 2025 (S12, S13).
Agro-waste: one agro-based biogas plant in Hoshiarpur, Punjab (S17).

subsections.title: How revenue is earned: segment mix and customers

blocks.caption: Revenue from operations by segment, Rs. crore (restated consolidated; converted from Rs. million in the abridged prospectus) (S2)

blocks.text: WWT is still the engine at about 67.5% of FY26 revenue, but it has not grown smoothly. WWT revenue fell about 10.5% in FY25 before recovering 15.7% in FY26, so the FY26 figure is only about 3.5% above FY24 (S2). Most incremental growth came from SWT, which nearly tripled from Rs.50.2 crore to Rs.140.2 crore over FY24-FY26 as the Goa plants scaled up (S2).

The customer base has two layers. In WWT and WRR, SFC's direct customers are mostly EPC companies that bid for municipal sewage-treatment and recycling tenders. The projects themselves are awarded by municipalities and government agencies (S2). Customers named in secondary summaries of the RHP include Enviro Control, Vishvaraj Environment, Ramky Infrastructure, EMS Limited and Enviro Infra Engineers (S15, S16). In SWT the customers are Goa Waste Management Corporation and oil marketing companies, the latter as buyers of compressed biogas (S2). Goa plant revenue comes from tipping fees, electricity sales, recyclables and remediation work (S16).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration and government dependence (S2)
rows: WWT + SWT share of total revenue

blocks.text: SFC's direct customers are private EPC contractors, but roughly 92% of WWT revenue and all SWT revenue ultimately trace back to government entities or tenders (S2). SFC carries municipal payment risk at one remove, which helps explain the long collection cycle discussed under Financials.

Directly and through subsidiaries, step-down subsidiaries and associates, SFC manufactures at Pune, Satara and Dombivli in Maharashtra and in the Czech Republic (S2). Because of the asset-light model, revenue per rupee of plant and equipment is high: fixed-asset turnover was 13.25x, 10.85x and 12.07x in FY24-FY26 (S2).

In Goa, the North Goa plant at Calangute, Bardez is run by subsidiary Hindustan Waste Treatment Pvt. Ltd. It was expanded from 100 to 250 TPD in 2022. The South Goa plant at Curchorem is run by wholly owned Vasudha Waste Treatment Pvt. Ltd. and has processed 100 TPD of mixed municipal waste since May 2023 (S16). The company states combined capacity of 425 TPD (S10, S17). Secondary pages list 250 + 100 TPD of processing capacity plus 75 TPD of handling capacity, which is how the 425 figure appears to be built up (S16).

items: Supply side: the RHP flags reliance on a few raw-material suppliers without exclusive agreements, and on contract labour for some operations (S15).
Seasonality: Indian WWT activity is seasonal and Q1 is structurally weak. Q1 FY26 revenue was only about 8% of the full year (S2, S15).
Foreign-exchange exposure from imported components and the European subsidiaries is flagged as a risk (S15).

blocks.text: In short: SFC is a technology-and-equipment supplier riding India's government-funded sewage-treatment build-out, with a Goa waste-to-energy operating business attached. It earns engineering-product margins but bears infrastructure-style receivable cycles.

The RHP's industry report (by F&S) sizes the global water and wastewater treatment market at USD 880 billion in CY2024 and USD 934 billion in CY2025. It projects USD 1,240 billion by CY2030E, a CAGR of about 5.8% (S2). The faster-growing niche relevant to SFC's WRR push is global tertiary treatment, valued at USD 1.40 billion in CY2024 and forecast to reach USD 4.34 billion by CY2031F, a 17.47% CAGR from CY2026E (S2).

For solid waste, the same report puts the revenue potential of India's municipal solid waste businesses at about Rs.217.4 billion in FY2026, rising to about Rs.329.2 billion by FY2031E, a CAGR of about 8.7% (S2). These are total-market figures from an issuer-commissioned report. They show the size of the opportunity, not SFC's addressable share.

blocks.caption: Industry figures cited in the RHP (F&S report) (S2)
rows: India municipal solid waste revenue potential

blocks.text: The RHP's listed peer set is Thermax, Praj Industries and Ion Exchange (S15). These are much larger, diversified environment, energy and water companies rather than like-for-like SBR technology suppliers, which reflects how few listed pure-play comparables exist. Several market sites also compare SFC with VA Tech Wabag, a water-technology EPC player, though it does not appear in the RHP peer set found (S15).

In practice, SFC competes at the level of process technology choice in municipal sewage tenders. The RHP's risk factors acknowledge that its products 'may be displaced by newer technology' and that competitors with better technology could take new orders (S2, S12). HDFC Sky's summary also lists SFC's moderate scale relative to larger domestic and international competitors as a risk (S16).

items: Listed peers named in the RHP: Thermax, Praj Industries, Ion Exchange (S15).
Frequently cited non-RHP comparable: VA Tech Wabag (S15).
Direct rivals in SBR and alternative STP technologies are not named in any source reviewed. This is a disclosure gap for investors.

blocks.text: There is a genuine, if narrow, moat. The over-80% share of India's SBR technology market comes from the issuer-commissioned F&S report, but it has been repeated consistently since the first DRHP in December 2024 (S14, S13, S15). It is backed by an installed base that grew from 577 to 728 plants (S2). An installed base this large, with roughly 92% of revenue from repeat customers, gives SFC reference sites, operating data and familiarity with EPC contractors and municipal engineers. That kind of advantage matters in conservative public procurement (S10, S2).

The limits are just as clear. The share claim covers one technology class (SBR), not the whole sewage-treatment market. SFC does not hold the end-customer relationship, which sits with municipalities and EPC firms. It has no long-term contracts with most of its top 10 customers. And its own RHP warns of technology displacement (S2). The WRR and SWT businesses are newer and have no comparable market-leadership claim (S2).

Verdict on moat: real but narrow. It is a specification and installed-base advantage within SBR sewage treatment, not a regulatory barrier or an import-substitution monopoly. It explains the steady ~29% EBITDA margins (S2), but it has not given SFC enough bargaining power to get paid on time.

Revenue grew at a 10.56% CAGR from FY24 to FY26, but PAT grew only about 5% a year, from Rs.144.2 crore to Rs.160.2 crore, and PAT margin slipped from 21.9% to 19.9% (S2, S7). EBITDA margin held at about 29.3-29.7% throughout, so the PAT dilution sits below the EBITDA line, consistent with rising borrowings and finance costs (S2). Return on equity fell from 29.8% to 21.6% as equity grew faster than profit (S2). (*Quarterly ROE is not annualised.)

Quarterly results are extremely seasonal. Q1 FY27 revenue doubled year on year to Rs.133.9 crore, but the quarter still produced only Rs.1.5 crore of PAT on a 7.4% EBITDA margin. Q1 FY26 was a small loss (S2, S11). The RHP itself attributes the quarterly pattern to seasonality and cyclicality (S2). The practical consequence is that most of each year's profit is booked late in the year, so a slip in Q4 execution or approvals moves the full-year number a lot.

The growth story is real but modest: about 10.6% revenue CAGR and about 5% PAT CAGR over two years (S2). Order-book growth (next subsection) is what supports a faster trajectory, not the historical P&L.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, cash flow and working capital

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash-flow indicators, Rs. crore unless stated (S2)

blocks.text: This is the most important table in the report. Over FY24-FY26 SFC reported cumulative PAT of about Rs.456 crore but generated only about Rs.28 crore of operating cash flow. Two of the three years were negative, and Q1 FY27 was negative again at -Rs.21.3 crore (S2). The cash conversion cycle widened from 156 to 242 days, and working capital went from about 40% to 65% of revenue (S2). The RHP lists negative operating cash flows and high working-capital needs among its top ten risk factors (S2).

Leverage is still low in absolute terms: net debt to equity is 0.05-0.08x. But the direction is wrong. Borrowings more than doubled in FY26, and the company moved from a net-cash to a net-debt position (S2). Financing inflows of Rs.92.5 crore in FY26 effectively funded the working-capital build and investing outflows. The company has also extended unsecured, recallable loans to six subsidiaries, which the RHP flags as a risk (S2).

Red flag: profit and cash flow do not match. About Rs.456 crore of three-year PAT produced only about Rs.28 crore of operating cash (S2). Profits locked in receivables owed, ultimately, by government-funded projects are lower-quality than the headline 20% PAT margin suggests.

subsections.title: Order book: does it support the growth story?

blocks.text: The order book nearly tripled in FY26 to Rs.1,574.5 crore, about 2x FY26 revenue (S2). By August 2026 it was split roughly into WWT Rs.641 crore, WRR Rs.561 crore and SWT Rs.454.5 crore (S11). That composition matters. A large share of the backlog now sits in WRR, where SFC booked its first revenue only in FY26, and in SWT/compressed biogas, where it cites Rs.501.7 crore of CBG orders (S2, S10, S11). These are newer businesses for SFC, so execution risk on the backlog is higher than in the core SBR business.

The RHP's order-book definition is broad. It includes letters of award, letters of intent, MoUs and 'other similar commitments' considered 'likely to fructify', plus long-term O&M contracts (S2). Investors should treat the headline figure as an upper bound on visible revenue rather than firm, funded orders.
Net assessment: the order book supports faster revenue growth than the 10.6% historical CAGR, but the trend in cash flow does not yet support the claim of a high-quality compounding business (S2).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key offer terms (S2, S7)
rows: 2,02,28,204 shares, about Rs.667.5 crore at upper band
QIB 50% (of which anchor 30% of issue), NII 15%, Retail 35%
IIFL Capital Services, JM Financial, Nuvama / MUFG Intime India

blocks.text: Most of the money raised goes to existing shareholders, not the company. OFS proceeds go to the selling shareholders after their share of issue expenses, and the company receives nothing from them (S2). Only the Rs.150 crore fresh issue, less issue expenses, reaches SFC (S2, S7).

This is the company's second attempt at listing. It first filed a DRHP with SEBI in December 2024 (fresh issue of Rs.185 crore plus an OFS of 1.08 crore shares), then filed a new DRHP dated August 25, 2025 (S4, S14, S3, S6). A corrigendum to the DRHP followed in December 2025, and the RHP was filed in October 2026 (S5, S1). SEBI's observation was reported on December 12, 2025 (S22). Between drafts the OFS grew from about 1.23 crore to 1.57 crore shares while the fresh issue stayed at Rs.150 crore (S17, S7).

subsections.title: Objects of the fresh issue, in full

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds from the Rs.150 crore fresh issue (S2)
rows: Prepayment of borrowings of the company and wholly owned subsidiary Vasudha Waste Treatment Pvt. Ltd.
To be finalised; capped at 25% of gross fresh proceeds (max Rs.37.5 crore)

blocks.text: None of the fresh money goes to capacity, manufacturing, technology or acquisitions. About Rs.117 crore is earmarked for repaying debt and funding working capital (S2, S7). Read with the cash-flow table, the IPO is partly a balance-sheet repair: it refinances the borrowings that funded the receivable build-up and pre-funds more working capital as the order book grows (S2). Debt repayment of Rs.42.2 crore covers about a fifth of the Rs.204.8 crore of June 2026 borrowings (S2).

The fresh issue does not buy growth assets. It buys time on working capital. That is not inherently bad for a business with a growing order book, but it means the investment case depends on SFC improving collections, not on new capacity.

subsections.title: Who is selling in the OFS

blocks.caption: Selling shareholders (S2, S7)
rows: Sandeep S. Asolkar (jointly with Priya Asolkar)

blocks.text: Promoter-director Dhandoriya is selling about 44% of his stake and executive director Sarvesh Garg about 64% of his. Three other early shareholders are each selling about 46% (S2). Their weighted average acquisition cost is Rs.36.72 per share, against a Rs.330 upper band (S2). The Asolkar family keeps most of its holding: the CMD's 1.35 crore directly held shares acquired at Rs.0.44 are not in the OFS (S2). The weighted average price of all share transactions in the past year was Rs.219.32, in a range of nil to Rs.343 (S2).

Founder Sandeep Sudhakar Asolkar, Chairman and MD, is a civil engineer from Sardar Patel College of Engineering (University of Bombay). He completed IIM Ahmedabad's Senior Management Programme and has over 31 years in environmental engineering. Before founding SFC he worked at Ion Exchange (India), Hindustan Dorr-Oliver, Gherzi Eastern and Klean Environmental Consultants (S2). This is directly relevant domain experience at India's established water-treatment firms.

Co-promoter Saketchandrasingh Dhandoriya, Executive Director, holds a mechanical engineering diploma and has 25+ years in environmental engineering. He has been with SFC since 2005, after serving as manager of field services at Ion Exchange (S2). Priya Asolkar, a civil engineer, has worked as a design engineer at several consultancies and as a consultant to SFC (S2). Prachiti Asolkar, the founder's daughter, has been an Executive Director since August 2023. She has a media-studies degree and master's degrees in finance and international business from Hult (S2). Her elevation is a family-succession move rather than a domain-experience appointment.

blocks.caption: Board and key managerial personnel (S2)
rows: Neha Rajen Gada, Mulesh Manilal Savla, Amruta Shripad Patankar, Divya Sameer Momaya

blocks.text: Promoter and promoter-group holding is 48.18% before the issue and 41.18% after, which is modest for a newly listed company (S7). The promoter group includes Asolkar Tradecraft Pvt. Ltd. with a 5.33% stake (S2). Half the board is independent (S2).

The abridged prospectus does not reproduce the RPT schedule, and the full RHP (over 10 MB) could not be retrieved, so the line-by-line RPT note was not reviewed. This is a gap. What is disclosed shows a group with many related entities: subsidiaries Hindustan Waste Treatment, Vasudha Waste Treatment, Fine Aeration Systems, Pentagen Biofuels, Sustainyx Smart Solution and SFC Umwelttechnik GmbH; subsidiary Chavare Engineering; and the Turbomax India joint venture (S2, S12).

items: Intra-group lending: SFC has extended unsecured loans, recallable at any time, to at least six subsidiaries, and the RHP warns they may not be able to repay on time (S2).
Fresh-issue proceeds will partly repay borrowings of Vasudha Waste Treatment, the South Goa plant subsidiary, so IPO money flows down into a subsidiary (S2).
Promoter-group entity Asolkar Tradecraft Pvt. Ltd. holds 5.33% pre-issue (S2). Its trading relationship with SFC, if any, could not be verified.
The RHP states there is no group-company litigation with a material impact on SFC (S2).

blocks.text: No promoter-linked supplier or customer was identified in the sources reviewed. The structure is mostly a web of operating subsidiaries funded by intra-group loans. That is typical for a company with PPP assets, but investors should read the RHP's RPT note before applying.

The RHP's own top-ten risk list includes an unusual admission: 'certain of our corporate records and filings are not traceable or have certain discrepancies', and the company cannot assure that regulators will not act or impose penalties (S2). Statutory auditors also included remarks, not qualifications, in their reports for FY24-FY26 (S2). Neither is fatal, but both point to weaker corporate housekeeping than at a typical mainboard issuer.

The criminal matter naming the company, the CMD and subsidiary HWTPL comes from a legal notice issued by Vikramaditya Shinde, a former HWTPL employee (S2). The largest exposure is material civil litigation involving German subsidiary SFC Umwelttechnik GmbH and others, at EUR 6.25 million, about Rs.66.7 crore. That is roughly 8% of FY26 net worth (S2). Subsidiaries also face 10 statutory or regulatory proceedings, which secondary summaries classify as environmental. Given that subsidiaries run waste-processing plants, these deserve attention (S2, S21). No SEBI or stock-exchange disciplinary action against promoters in the last five years is disclosed (S2).

items: 1. Persistent cash-flow shortfall. Operating cash flow was negative in FY24, FY26 and Q1 FY27, and the RHP says it 'may continue to have negative cash flows in the future'. Cumulative three-year OCF is about Rs.28 crore against about Rs.456 crore of PAT (S2).

2. Working-capital intensity rising faster than revenue. The cash conversion cycle went from 156 to 242 days and working capital from 40% to 65% of revenue over two years, funded partly by new borrowings (S2).
3. Extreme seasonality. Q1 produced 7% EBITDA margins and near-zero profit in both of the last two years, so annual results depend on a strong second half (S2).

blocks.text: Together these three risks mean a single delayed municipal payment cycle, or a weak fourth quarter, could hit both reported profit and liquidity. The IPO's working-capital allocation of Rs.74.9 crore softens but does not remove this risk (S2).

items: 4. Government dependence. 92.35% of FY26 WWT revenue and 100% of SWT revenue is directly or indirectly attributable to government entities or tenders. Any change in funding programmes or payment discipline flows straight through (S2).
5. Customer concentration with no long-term contracts. Top-5 customers were 47.1% of FY26 revenue and 62.1% in Q1 FY27, and SFC lacks long-term contracts with most top-10 customers (S2).
6. Technology displacement. The RHP's first-listed risk is that products 'may be displaced by newer technology'. The moat rests on one process technology, SBR (S2).

7. Execution risk on the new backlog. Over half of the August 2026 order book is in WRR (Rs.561 crore) and SWT (Rs.454.5 crore), where SFC's operating history is short. WRR booked its first revenue in FY26 (S11, S2). Local Goa press has reported the Cacora (South Goa) plant running at a fraction of its 100 TPD capacity because of low waste feed. These reports are undated and may be stale, but they show utilisation risk at the PPP plants (S23).

blocks.text: Concentration is getting worse, not better: top-5 customer share rose every period from 40.5% in FY24 to 62.1% in Q1 FY27 (S2).

items: 8. Corporate-record discrepancies and litigation. The RHP admits some corporate records are untraceable or discrepant, and there is EUR 6.25 million (about Rs.66.7 crore) of material civil litigation at the German subsidiary plus 10 regulatory matters against subsidiaries (S2).
Intra-group exposure: unsecured, recallable loans to six subsidiaries could prove hard to recover (S2).
Post-listing overhang: anchors hold 60.7 lakh shares, with 50% unlocking on 29 Nov 2026 and the rest on 28 Jan 2027 (S7).

blocks.text: Excluded as boilerplate: generic first-issue price risk, forex, contract labour and sanctions/anti-bribery compliance. They are disclosed in the RHP but do not distinguish this issuer (S2, S15).

Management's forward-looking statements in the offer document are qualitative strategy statements, not numerical guidance (S2). No investor call or media interview giving revenue, margin or cash-flow targets was found during this research. The outlook below is the company's stated intent, not a forecast.

items: Expand SWT through large-scale projects and move into agro-waste projects, building on the Hoshiarpur agro-biogas plant (S2, S17).
Forward integration into wastewater recycling and reuse with innovative technologies (WRR), supported by the DuPont supply agreement (S2, S18).
Further strengthen the core WWT business (S2).
Acquisitions and expansion into new geographies, following the 2025 purchase of 80% of IST-Anlagenbau (S2, S12).
Increase R&D to commercialise more technologies (S2).

blocks.text: The concrete forward evidence is the order book: Rs.1,570.1 crore at June 30, 2026, about 2x FY26 revenue (S2). By August 2026 it was split into WWT Rs.641 crore, WRR Rs.561 crore and SWT Rs.454.5 crore (S11), with compressed-biogas orders of Rs.501.7 crore cited as a diversification avenue (S10).

If the backlog converts, FY27-FY28 revenue growth should run ahead of the 10.6% FY24-FY26 CAGR (S2). But the mix shift is toward WRR and CBG/SWT, which are larger-ticket, more project-like and newer for SFC. These businesses are likely to need more working capital and carry more execution risk than the asset-light SBR supply model (S2, S11). Nothing in the disclosures suggests management expects the cash conversion cycle to shorten, and the IPO itself allocates Rs.74.9 crore to fund more working capital (S2).

Bottom line: there is a credible growth runway from the order book, but no management commitment on cash conversion. Investors should watch the first two listed half-year results for operating cash flow, not revenue.

subsections.title: Subscription so far, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: This report is written on day 2 of a three-day issue (closing 29 October 2026), so the figures below are partial and will change materially on the final day, when QIB bids usually arrive. At the end of day 1 the issue was 0.10x subscribed overall: retail 0.16x, NII 0.09x and QIB effectively nil (S9, S10). As of 5:05 pm on 28 October (day 2) it had reached 0.27x overall (S8).

Anchor book: on 26 October SFC allotted 60,68,460 shares at Rs.330 to anchor investors, raising Rs.200.26 crore. Mutual funds took 89.14%, FPIs 5.87% and insurers 4.99%. Named participants include SBI MF, Nippon India MF and ICICI Prudential MF (S7, S9). Half the anchor shares are locked in until 29 November 2026 and the rest until 28 January 2027 (S7).

Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated and not an investment signal): Investorgain reported Rs.13 on the evening of 28 October, down from a peak of about Rs.32 on 24 October (S19). GMPIPOWatch showed Rs.21 at its last update (S20). The trend is falling alongside subdued two-day demand.

method: Primary source: the 14-page Abridged Prospectus of the RHP dated 19 Oct 2026, downloaded from SEBI and read page by page (S2). It supplied the segment revenue, customer concentration, government dependence, restated financials including cash flows, KPIs (order book, cash conversion cycle), objects of the issue, the OFS table with acquisition costs, promoter biographies, the board, the top-10 risk factors and the litigation summary. The full RHP (sfcenvironment.com) and the August 2025 DRHP both exceed the 10 MB fetch limit, and downloading them by shell needed permissions that were not available. As a result, the full Business, Industry, MD&A and Related-Party-Transactions chapters were NOT read directly. Gaps that follow: the line-by-line RPT schedule, named competitors beyond the RHP peer list, Goa concession tenure and renewal terms, and supplier names. Customer names, the >80% SBR share claim, Goa plant capacities, the August 2026 segment order book and the repeat-customer share come from secondary summaries of the RHP, cross-checked where possible across at least two of S10, S11, S13, S14, S15 and S16. Rs. crore figures were converted from the abridged prospectus's Rs. million figures and derived ratios (cumulative OCF vs PAT, segment shares, OFS stake percentages) were computed by the analyst. Subscription figures are partial (day 2 of 3). GMP is unofficial and was not used in the verdict. Valuation was deliberately excluded, and P/E figures seen in sources were omitted. Some secondary pages (S12, S15, S16, S18-S21, S23) have no visible publication date, so the access date is recorded. S23 is a search-result headline only, has no date and may be stale. One secondary page (S15) is internally inconsistent about the business, and Groww (S18) mislabels Rs. million as Rs. crore, so only uncontested facts were taken from them.
